newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Industrial, transport chaos looms in South Korea.
newsitem.headline: Industrial, transport chaos looms in South Korea.

text.p: Striking South Korean workers shut car factories and shipyards on Thursday, crippling key export industries, and hospital and subway workers threatened to join an all-out work stoppage in fury at a new labour law.

An initial half a million workers were called out on an indefinte strike by a militant union body in response to the surprise passage of a law that challenges decades of job security by allowing worker layoffs.
A more moderate union group instructed its 1.2 million members to join them on Friday.
As the prospect of industrial and transport chaos loomed, the government warned of "stern countermeasures".
"We are hoisting the flag of a general strike to punish outrages of the Kim Young-sam government," the more moderate Federation of Korean Trade Unions said in a statement.
Opposition deputies occupied parliament in a silent sit-down protest and vowed to remain there until midnight on Saturday.

They said they would mount a constitutional challenge to the labour law and to another controversial bill passed at the same time that strengthens the domestic intelligence agency, once the scourge of political dissidents.
Only members of Kim's ruling New Korea Party were called to vote on the bills in a dawn session of the National Assembly.
The outlawed Korea Confederation of Trade Unions ordered work stoppages at 300 companies. Workers at Hyundai Motor, Kia Motors and Ssangyong Motor responded, halting production.

Shipyard workers at Hyundai Heavy, Hyundai Mipo Dockyards, Halla Heavy Industries and Hanjin Heavy Industries also walked off the job. Unionised yard workers at Daewoo Heavy Industries voted to down tools on Friday.
Vehicles and ships are South Korea's big export items and have underpinned its rise as an Asian "tiger" economy.
Union workers in at least 13 hospitals, including Seoul National University Hospital, the country's leading medical centre, elected to strike on Friday.
More than 9,000 Seoul subway workers will walk off the job on Saturday, a half day for most Korean workers.
The Federation of Korean Trade Unions said its initial stoppage would begin at 1.00 p.m. (0400 GMT) on Friday and last until noon (0300 GMT) on Saturday. Further action may follow.
"Workers have nothing to lose any more," said Namuh Rhee, the head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities. "I see a series of massive strikes in the first quarter of 1997.
"But later on, the government will get support of the public, because when Koreans feel they are in crisis they tend to rally around the government."
New Korea Party chairman Lee Hong-koo said adoption of the hotly debated bills was "regrettable but inevitable".
The party has an absolute majority in the National Assembly, but generally seeks compromise with opposition groups on its legislative agenda.
"The people will decide which side was right next year," Lee said, referring to presidential elections next December.

"The government expresses serious worries over the impact on the national economy and has decided to take stern countermeasures against these illegal actions," Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung's office said in a statement.

Stocks have tumbled on fears of strike damage to an already shaky economy. But analysts said the labour law, which allows companies to lay off workers and introduce flexible work hours, would help in the long term by cutting costs.
An angry opposition National Congress for New Politics condemned what it called a "Kim Young-sam coup" and said it would join the United Liberal Democrats to fight the laws.

The bill giving wider powers to the National Security Planning Agency has been attacked by the opposition as a ploy by Kim to crack down on his foes ahead of next December's vote. Kim cannot run for a second term but will anoint a successor.

South Korea's version of the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency was stripped of many of its investigative powers by Kim under an election pledge to curb the agency once notorious for torture and kidnapping.
The ruling party insists the agency must be given sharper teeth to combat a renewed threat of subversion from Pyongyang.
